journals.title: David Roberts Welsh Journal
journals.sourceTitle: FAMILY HISTORY, WRITINGS AND POEMS of DAVID ROBERTS, NATIVE OF LLANFROTHEN, MEIRIONETHSHIRE, WALES
journals.primaryWriter: David Roberts and later Roberts family contributors
journals.language: Primarily Welsh, with later English additions and inserted printed material
journals.description: One physically two-ended family volume containing Welsh poetry and other writings, a Welsh family-history and journal sequence, later family additions, and inserted printed material.
journals.sourceIdentityNote: This is one physical source begun by David Roberts and later continued, copied, translated, annotated, or supplemented by Roberts family contributors. The site does not attribute the entire volume to one hand.
journals.physicalStructureNote: Verified PDF structure: covers on pages 1 and 110; poetry/writings on pages 2-62; inserted/printed poetry on pages 63-66; family-history title leaf on page 67; family-history/journal sequence on pages 68-109.
journals.exportStatus: Welsh transcription, modern English translation, bilingual Word, and combined PDF exports are defined for later generation from these same page Markdown files; they are not published as complete while nearly all pages remain untranscribed.

attributionModel.historicalConstraint: David Roberts died November 4, 1858; post-death material is not attributed as newly written by him.

journalPages.welshTranscription:
[Untranscribed: Welsh handwriting above the pasted title label.]

FAMILY HISTORY, WRITINGS AND POEMS
of
DAVID ROBERTS, NATIVE OF
LLANFROTHEN, MEIRIONETHSHIRE, WALES
He was the first
PRESIDENT OF THE FESTINIOG, WALES,
BRANCH OF THE CHURCH OF JESUS CHRIST
OF LATTER DAY SAINTS

D. R. Roberts
Ogden Utah
Chairman
Aug. 1948

journalPages.contentContext: Family-history title leaf. The pasted label identifies David Roberts and the Llanfrothen/Festiniog context; Welsh writing above the label is preserved separately from the English label.
journalPages.editor: D. R. Roberts (as written; identity unresolved)
journalPages.attributionBasis: A pasted title label is signed D. R. Roberts and dated Aug. 1948; the signer's identity is unresolved.

Logan City
January 2, 1861

Rhoddaf ychydig o ein hanes o'r
hen wlad hyd Gymru hyd yn awr, mor
gywir ac y mae fy nghof yn gallu.
Darfu ni ymadael o Festiniog Bethania yn
flwyddyn 1856, a o Ebrill 14 a chyrhaeddasom
Liverpool ac ar y 19 o'r un mis aethom i'r
llong S. Curling, yr hon oedd yn cychwyn ei
thaith dros Môr yr Iwerydd, drannoeth bu y daith
hon yn lled fawr, y môr yn codi iawn gyffelybasom
gyfandir America, ar y 24 o Mai. [unclear: niw y lle]
cyntaf [unclear: darfu ni] Boston. yn [unclear: rhyw] ddiwrnod
neu ddau darfu ni gymeryd Cerbydres, i deithio
oddiyno i Iowa-City, buom yma am yn agos
i dair wythnos o amser, ar lle hyn y cychwynom
gymeryd ein daith dros y gwastadedd ar
handcart hefo y llaw trocha i Utah. Darfu ni
aros ychydig y lle hwn sef Dinas y
Llyn Halen ar y 2 dydd o Hydref; bu y
daith hon yn galed iawn o herwydd nad oedd
gennym hanner digon o fwyd a [unclear: phriodoldeb] caled i
dynu y llaw troli. Darfu ni aros yma

journalPages.translation:
Logan City, January 2, 1861.

I will give a little of our history from the old country up to the present, as correctly as my memory allows. We left Bethania, Ffestiniog, on April 14, 1856, and reached Liverpool. On the nineteenth of the same month we went aboard the ship *S. Curling*, which began its journey across the Atlantic the following day. The voyage was very rough, with the sea rising greatly. We reached the American continent on May 24, [unclear in Welsh] Boston. After a day or two we took the railroad to Iowa City, where we remained for nearly three weeks. From there we began our journey across the plains with handcarts to Utah.

We stayed for a few days in Salt Lake City after arriving on October 2. The journey was very hard because we did not have half enough food, and pulling the handcart was hard. After several days my father and the [unclear in Welsh] went to Farmington, eighteen miles north of Salt Lake City. I then went twenty-two miles farther to Ogden with Erastus Bingham and remained there for four [unclear in Welsh], after which I returned to my father, my mother, my brothers, and my sisters.

[The opening Welsh words are unclear.] My father spent the whole time watching with a man because of his feet, since his boots were too small. Thomas worked with [unclear name: James Lathad] and received ten bushels of wheat and some clothing for his work. Daniel stayed with Lot Smith and received [unclear in Welsh] for his work. Ann and Elizabeth were in service, and Jane was at home.

In 1858 we moved south with the Saints. We borrowed food from William Richard, which was repaid to him in 1859. We were in the South for nearly two months, then returned and earned a little wheat by working. My father and I went to the canyons to make shingles. After about a month my mother and Thomas were seized by an illness. My father had to remain home to watch over them, and I went to the soldiers' camp to seek work, but I did not prosper and returned. My mother and brother were no better. They began to improve after a week, but my father, Daniel, Ann, and Jane then took their place; the illness did not affect Elizabeth.

This disease ended my father's life on this earth. We buried him in the Farmington cemetery. My father died in 1858. After returning from his funeral I took to my bed and was unable to rise without help for nearly three months. In [unclear in Welsh], in the month of April...

journalPages.translation:

I set out for the gold mines, thinking that I could earn money to pay our debt, but I did not go there. I remained at Fort Bridger to work for the soldiers and build some [unclear in Welsh]. I then returned to my mother, my brothers, and my sisters, and nearly all our debt was paid. My brother had earned some wheat.

At the end of October I set out to look for land that could be cultivated so that we could raise our own bread and potatoes. I stayed in Cache Valley, [unclear in Welsh] at Logan, and worked there for a short time. My brother Thomas came after me and made an agreement with a man named Shepherd. [The following travel and employment wording is unclear in Welsh.]

Thomas and I returned home after February in the year 1860. We had to remain there because our animals were weak and we had little fodder for them. At the end of March we began our journey again. Daniel remained in Farmington to work and came after us shortly afterward. We raised only a small crop: 59 bushels of wheat, 4 bushels of barley, 15 bushels [unclear crop], 10 bushels of potatoes, and a few other things. We have prospered well from the year 1859 until now [continues on PDF page 80].
